claim: Fine-grained, internal token-probability confidence scores (minimum token probability, lowest-K token probability, attention-weighted uncertainty) separate correct from incorrect code revisions far better than sequence-level scores (normalised sequence likelihood, average token probability).
stance_target: internal/logit signals as the load-bearing correctness signal for code, contra verbalized confidence
scope_conditions: automated code revision (program repair, vulnerability repair, code refinement), 14 models
quoted_support: minimum token probability yields the widest separation (EM-W1: 0.13-0.26, EP-W1: 0.13-0.20), whilst sequence-level confidence scores have a separation of 0.01-0.03 for the majority of models against both correctness metrics.

claim: Global Platt-scaling, a post-hoc recalibration standard for code generation tasks, is known to be ineffective specifically for program repair.
stance_target: limits of post-hoc calibration for code, motivating alternative (e.g. train-time) approaches
quoted_support: existing post-hoc calibration approaches such as Platt-scaling ... have been found to be ineffective for program repair and have not yet been evaluated on core tasks like vulnerability repair and automated code refinement.

claim: Token-level softmax probabilities for LLM-generated code revisions exhibit strong negative skewness across all models and tasks studied, meaning low-probability outlier tokens (not the bulk of high-probability tokens) carry the correctness signal.
stance_target: mechanism explaining why sequence-level averaging destroys discriminative signal for code
scope_conditions: automated code revision, all 14 models tested
quoted_support: the distributions of softmax probabilities consistently exhibit strong negative skewness for all models and tasks. This indicates that low softmax probabilities are consistently centred around a few outlier tokens in the generated code revisions.

claim: This paper's confidence signal is exclusively internal/logit-derived and post-hoc calibrated; it never elicits or trains a verbalized/natural-language confidence expression from the model.
stance_target: claim that verbalized/train-time code confidence calibration is already covered by this paper
quoted_support: we propose three fine-grained confidence scores: minimum token probability, lowest-K token probability, and attention-weighted uncertainty, and compare them with two traditional sequence-level confidence scores: normalised sequence likelihood and average token probability.
